name: Hana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Elmfield Primary, a state school on the edge of town, so thirty eight- and nine-year-olds all day. Phonics catch-up at quarter to nine, maths, English, then the afternoon is science or art or whatever the timetable throws at us. I'm in the same room with the same kids from morning to home time, which I love. You really get to know them.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Keeping six different reading levels going at once. I've got a boy who reads like a twelve-year-old and three who are still sounding out words. Sometimes I use an AI tool to make three versions of the same worksheet, which saves me an evening, but I always check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and it's still a handy little helper. I'd probably share a worksheet trick in the staff group chat. Nothing more dramatic than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, and they're pretty good. I'm on decent pay for a class teacher and Tom's accountancy job carries on. We've got about eight months saved, so I'd feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. I'd keep using the tool on Sunday evenings for differentiated worksheets and keep checking every line. And I'd keep putting money aside, because Tom and I want to buy a place before we have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal September, busy but nothing to be scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI tool for worksheets. Would you keep using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's useful for boring stuff. The AI tool turned a story about Roman roads into three reading levels in two minutes. One version had a Roman eating a potato, so I check everything now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still on your mind in that world, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. Our landlord put it up by eighty a month this year. But that's annoying, not frightening, with what we've saved.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** and still a handy helper.
I'd share a **worksheet trick** with colleagues in the staff chat.
think: Our life stays **pretty good**, with my pay and Tom's accountancy job.
Eight months of **savings** make me feel secure.
do: Keep using AI for **Sunday worksheets**, checking every single line before printing.
Keep saving each month towards a **flat deposit** with Tom.
S0.quote: The AI tool turned a story about Roman roads into three reading levels in two minutes. One version had a Roman eating a potato, so I check everything now.
fieldNote: She's a **careful user** of AI, already checking its mistakes.
The only pressure she names is **rent rises**, which savings absorb.
Her household feels **secure** with two steady incomes.

steps.text: Make three reading levels of each worksheet with AI, then check
Save monthly towards a deposit on a flat with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should help teachers, not replace teaching assistants. I'd want the union and the council to set rules on it. Online I'd probably share articles about fair pay for workers whose jobs change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly fine. A Year 4 class still needs a grown-up to tie shoelaces and stop a fight over the glue stick. The person I'd worry about is Tom, because checking numbers is exactly what this card describes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on a proper AI course once the school offers one, after a few colleagues tried it. We'd stop looking at bigger flats and save harder, maybe £300 a month more. And I'd go to the union meeting about how AI gets used in planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Fine about myself, a knot in my stomach about Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Tom's work. Where does he fit in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right in the middle of it. He spends his days checking expense claims and doing month-end accounts for small firms. If software does that, his firm needs fewer people like him, and he's only two years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom to start learning the software now, before his boss buys it. And that we'd be okay on my salary for a while. I'd mean it, but I'd still be nervous.

say: I'd say AI should **help teachers**, not cut assistants.
I'd want **union and council** rules on how schools use it.
think: My **classroom job** looks safe, because children need adults.
Tom's **accountancy work** is exactly the checking AI takes first.
do: Join a **school AI course** once colleagues have tried it.
Save an extra **£300 a month** instead of renting bigger.
feel: Fine for herself, but a **knot** in her stomach about Tom.
S1.quote: A Year 4 class still needs a grown-up to tie shoelaces and stop a fight over the glue stick.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe; the **household risk** is her partner's income.
She's **steady**: she'll learn the tools once others have proved them.
Her politics show in wanting **rules** and protection for assistants.

steps.text: Sign up for the school's AI training after colleagues try it
Put an extra £300 a month into savings
Attend the union meeting on AI in lesson planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now, with a safety net for everyone whose job goes. I'd be on every petition about it. You can't let a few companies decide what happens to millions of families in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Tom loses his job in that first year. And I'm not sure about mine anymore either, because if AI can teach reading as well as me, someone will try it on a budget. We'd be down to one income, maybe less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit plan and keep every penny liquid. Tom would start looking at jobs that need a person, maybe something in the council or retraining. I'd join the union's campaign for ratios and stick close to the parents, because they'd fight for real teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not panicky, but properly scared, because it's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your own day is thinking work, and how much is hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, marking and reports are thinking work, maybe half my week. The rest is in the room: hands-on with kids, reading with them, wiping noses, dealing with tears. So AI takes half my job in 2028 and the robots come in 2031, but parents won't want a robot doing playtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd put off having a baby for a few years. Putting off a baby would upset me more than the money.

say: I'd demand a **safety net** for everyone whose job goes.
I'd sign **every petition** for limits on AI companies.
think: I think Tom **loses his job** in the first year.
My own teaching could be **trialled cheaply** by budget-cutters.
do: Pause the **deposit plan** and keep savings in cash.
Join the union's **ratio campaign** and build support with parents.
feel: Properly **scared**, because both incomes are at risk at once.
S2.quote: We'd put off having a baby for a few years. Putting off a baby would upset me more than the money.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose work, which makes this alarmed.
Half her week is **hands-on**, which buys her some years.
The real cost to her is **delaying children**, not money.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and hold savings in cash
Campaign with the union and parents for teacher ratios
Delay plans for a first baby by a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan properly: retraining money, shorter weeks, protections in law. I'd push our union to get ahead of it. I'd share that kind of thing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay, because primary kids need people. Tom has time to move, which changes everything. It's worrying, but not like the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would start a part-time qualification in something people-facing, maybe financial advice, in year one. I'd do the AI course and use it for planning so I'm not left behind. We'd probably still buy a small flat, just not the one with the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. Like an exam you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom do with five years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means my partner Tom can retrain before it hits, while we still have two salaries. That's the big one. I'd also start reading up on whatever comes after, so I'm not guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your own teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the bits only a person can do: reading with children, nature walks, drama. I'd let AI write my plans and reports so I have more time for that.

say: I'd ask for **retraining money**, shorter weeks and protections in law.
I'd push our **union** to plan ahead instead of reacting late.
think: I'd be okay, because **primary children** need people.
Five years gives Tom **time to move**, which changes everything.
do: Help Tom start a **part-time qualification** in the first year.
Use AI for **plans and reports** to free time for children.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like an exam she knows is coming.
S3.quote: Five years means my partner Tom can retrain before it hits, while we still have two salaries.
fieldNote: The extra years mainly help her **partner**, not her.
She'd hand **paperwork** to AI and keep the human bits.
Still anxious, because Tom's income **could go**.

steps.text: Use AI to write weekly plans and end-of-term reports
Support Tom through a part-time financial advice course
Buy a smaller flat without a garden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right. Ten years is enough to plan for teachers and families. I'd keep talking about fair rules, but without the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37. Probably still teaching, maybe a deputy head. I'd have time to see how other schools use it and copy what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep saving. I'd learn the tools steadily, maybe one new thing a term. And we'd go ahead and have kids on our normal timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly okay. It's on my mind, not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot part, around 2039, matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really for me. By then I'd hope parents still want a real teacher. If robots can do playtime, we've got bigger problems than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still teaching, with a toddler at home. Tom would have moved into something safer by then. That's my hope, anyway.

fieldNote: A decade lets her keep **family plans** on track.
She expects to keep teaching, maybe **promoted**.

steps.text: Learn one new AI planning tool each term

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us would be hit at once. What would help is a real safety net, so losing a job doesn't mean losing your home. And support for people like Tom to retrain without a gap in pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the children. My class are eight. They'll be twenty when all this lands, and nobody's teaching them for that world yet.

Fast AGI **alarms** her because both incomes would wobble and baby plans would slip.
With more warning, she'd help Tom **retrain** and keep her family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes would be hit at once.
